Comparing an enum with a raw value, as in `status === 1`, ties the code to the number behind the member. If you reorder the enum or insert a member, the comparison means something else and you get no compile error.

The rule checks `==`, `!=`, `===`, `!==`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and the `case` labels of a `switch`. Comparing members of two different enums is reported too.

`bun lint --type-aware` turns this rule on in TypeScript files.

{/* Generated by src/codegen/lint-rule-docs.ts. Do not edit this section. */}

## Configure

Off by default. This rule needs types, so turning it on makes `bun lint` type check your code first.

```toml bunfig.toml
[lint.rules]
"@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-enum-comparison" = "error" # or "warn"
```

{/* End of the generated section. */}

## Examples

Reported:

{/* bad {"count": 3} */}
```ts
enum Status {
  Open,
  Closed,
}

enum Color {
  Red = "red",
}

function describe(status: Status, color: Color) {
  if (status === 1) {
    return "closed";
  }
  if (color === "red") {
    return "red";
  }
  switch (status) {
    case 0:
      return "open";
  }
}
```

Not reported:

{/* good */}
```ts
enum Status {
  Open,
  Closed,
}

enum Color {
  Red = "red",
}

function describe(status: Status, color: Color) {
  if (status === Status.Closed) {
    return "closed";
  }
  if (color === Color.Red) {
    return "red";
  }
  switch (status) {
    case Status.Open:
      return "open";
  }
}
```

A comparison with another kind of value, such as `undefined`, isn't reported:

{/* good */}
```ts
enum Status {
  Open,
  Closed,
}

function isSet(status?: Status) {
  return status !== undefined;
}
```
